classification.difficultyReason: Counts unordered group partitions by cases and avoids double-counting equal-sized groups.

content.prompt: Six people are to be divided into two groups, each with at least one person. Assume that all divisions into two unlabelled groups are equally likely.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Explain why the total possible ways to do this is 31.

answer.worked:
The possible group sizes are $(1,5)$, $(2,4)$ and $(3,3)$. Choosing one group determines the other. For $(3,3)$, divide by 2 because choosing either group gives the same division.
$$\begin{aligned}N&={}^{6}C_1+{}^{6}C_2+\frac{{}^{6}C_3}{2}\\&=6+15+10\\&=31.\end{aligned}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: Find the probability that there will be three in each group,

answer.worked:
There are $\frac{{}^{6}C_3}{2}=10$ divisions into two groups of three.
$$P(3,3)=\frac{{}^{6}C_3/2}{31}=\frac{10}{31}.$$

children.label: c
children.prompt: Find the probability that there will be two in one group and four in the other,

answer.worked:
Choose the two-person group; the remaining four form the other group.
$$P(2,4)=\frac{{}^{6}C_2}{31}=\frac{15}{31}.$$

children.label: d
children.prompt: Find the probability that there will be one group of five and an individual.

answer.worked:
Choose the individual; the other five form the remaining group.
$$P(1,5)=\frac{{}^{6}C_1}{31}=\frac{6}{31}.$$
